---
title: "Bayesian null fitting with MCMC"
subtitle: "Credible intervals for a calibrated p-value"
---

## The uncertainty the point estimate hides

`fitNull` returns a single $(\hat\mu, \hat\sigma)$, and `calibrateP` then treats
those two numbers as if they were known. They are not — they are estimated from
a few dozen negative controls, and as the simulation on the
[empirical null](null-distribution.qmd#what-the-number-of-controls-buys-you)
page shows, that estimate can be loose.

A calibrated p-value of 0.04 computed from a null fitted on 20 controls and one
fitted on 200 are not the same claim, but nothing in the output distinguishes
them. `fitMcmcNull` samples the posterior of $(\mu, \tau)$ instead of maximising
the likelihood, so that uncertainty propagates all the way through to a credible
interval on the p-value itself.

## The posterior

Parameterise by the precision $\tau = 1/\sigma^2$. The likelihood is the one
from the [empirical null](null-distribution.qmd#the-likelihood):

$$
L(\mu, \tau) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{n}
\phi\!\left(\hat\beta_i \;;\; \mu,\ \sqrt{\tau^{-1} + \hat\sigma_i^2}\right).
$$

The priors are deliberately weak — the intent is to report the information in
the controls, not to add to it:

$$
\pi(\mu) \;\propto\; 1,
\qquad
\tau \;\sim\; \mathrm{Gamma}\!\left(10^{-4},\, 10^{-4}\right),
$$

a flat prior on the mean and the standard near-improper gamma on the precision
(mean 1, variance $10^{4}$). The log posterior is therefore the log likelihood
plus $\log \mathrm{Gamma}(\tau; 10^{-4}, 10^{-4})$, which is what
`logLikelihoodNullMcmc` computes.

## The sampler

A Metropolis random walk with a symmetric normal proposal, so the acceptance
ratio is just the posterior ratio:

$$
\alpha \;=\; \min\!\left(1,\ \frac{\pi(\mu', \tau' \mid \text{data})}{\pi(\mu, \tau \mid \text{data})}\right).
$$

Two implementation details worth knowing:

**The precision is reflected, not rejected.** A proposal with $\tau' < 0$ is
replaced by $\lvert\tau'\rvert$ rather than discarded. Reflection at a boundary
preserves the symmetry of the proposal, so the Metropolis ratio stays valid.

**The proposal scale is set by profile likelihood, not tuned by hand.** Before
sampling, the chain starts from the posterior mode (found by the same
Nelder–Mead used in `fitNull`), and the step size for each parameter is set to
the distance from the mode at which the profile log-likelihood has dropped by
$\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^2_{1}(0.9) \approx 1.35$ — located by binary search. That is a
cheap proxy for the posterior's own scale in each direction, and it means the
sampler adapts to the data rather than to a default.

```{python}
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]

ec.set_seed(123)
null = ec.fitMcmcNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr, iter=100_000)
print(null)
```

Note what the printed object reports: the posterior median of the mean, and the
posterior median of the **precision** — not the standard deviation. To get
$\sigma$, take $1/\sqrt{\tau}$.

```{python}
import numpy as np

chain = null.mcmc["chain"]
sigma = 1 / np.sqrt(chain[:, 1])
print(f"posterior median sigma: {np.median(sigma):.3f}")
print(f"95% credible interval:  {np.quantile(sigma, 0.025):.3f} - "
      f"{np.quantile(sigma, 0.975):.3f}")
print(f"acceptance rate:        {float(np.mean(null.mcmc['acc'])):.2f}")
```

## Checking the chain

An acceptance rate near the 0.2–0.5 range and traces that mix without drift are
the minimum bar. `plotMcmcTrace` shows both parameters:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Trace of the mean and precision. Look for a stationary band with no trend and no long flat stretches."
fig = ec.plotMcmcTrace(null)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## No burn-in is discarded

`fitMcmcNull` returns the entire chain including its first iterations, and the
posterior summaries are quantiles over all of it. This follows the R package's
behaviour exactly. Because the chain is started at the posterior mode rather
than at an arbitrary point, the burn-in problem is much reduced — but if you
want to be careful, summarise `null.mcmc["chain"]` yourself after dropping the
first few thousand rows.
:::

## Calibrating against it

Pass the `McmcNull` to `calibrateP`. The calibration formula is applied once per
posterior draw, and the result is summarised by its median and 2.5%/97.5%
quantiles:

```{python}
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]
ec.calibrateP(null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)
```

The interval is a **credible interval for the calibrated p-value** — the range
of p-values consistent with the posterior uncertainty about the null. A wide one
is a signal that you do not have enough negative controls to make a confident
calibrated claim in either direction.

Passing `pValueOnly=True` returns just the median p-values as an array, matching
`calibrateP` on a plain `Null`.

The same posterior propagates into the [EASE](ease.qmd) summary and into
[LLR calibration](maxsprt.qmd), both of which accept an `McmcNull` and return
intervals rather than points.

## Cost

The default is 100,000 iterations, each requiring a full pass over the negative
controls. This is the slowest of the fitting routines by a wide margin — seconds
to tens of seconds where `fitNull` is instantaneous. For exploratory work
`iter=10_000` is usually enough to see whether the credible interval is wide or
narrow; keep the default for anything you report.

Because the sampler draws from a port of R's Mersenne-Twister,
`ec.set_seed(n)` reproduces R's `set.seed(n)` stream exactly, so a given seed
gives the same chain in both languages — see [Validation](../validation.qmd).

## API

| Function | Use |
|---|---|
| [`fitMcmcNull(logRr, seLogRr, iter=100000)`](../reference/index.qmd#fitmcmcnull) | Sample the posterior; returns an `McmcNull`. |
| [`calibrateP(mcmcNull, ...)`](../reference/index.qmd#calibratep) | Calibrated p-value with a credible interval. |
| [`plotMcmcTrace(mcmcNull)`](../reference/index.qmd#plotmcmctrace) | Trace plots for both parameters. |
| `null.mcmc["chain"]` | The raw $(\mu, \tau)$ draws, for your own summaries. |
